procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be a lower court in Andhra Pradesh since the High Court heard an appeal.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated September 18, 1963, of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 385 of 1962.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Andhra Pradesh High Court convicted Purna Chandra Rao under s. 342 of the Indian Penal Code but released him under s. 562(1-A) of the Criminal Procedure Code after admonition. The High Court also released A.K. Mallu (the respondent in one appeal) after admonition under s. 562(1-A) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Two appeals were filed in the Supreme Court. Criminal Appeal No. 243 of 1964 was filed by Purna Chandra Rao (who was convicted but released with admonition). Criminal Appeal No. 65 of 1964 was filed by A.K. Mallu against the High Court's judgment releasing the respondent (Purna Chandra Rao) after admonition. The Supreme Court dismissed both appeals. The appeal of A.K. Mallu was dismissed in default after his advocate withdrew from the case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the phrase 'any offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment' in Section 562(1-A) of the Criminal Procedure Code should be interpreted ejusdem generis with the preceding specific offences, thereby limiting its application to offences relating to property.

facts: An accused person was convicted of wrongful confinement under Section 342 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
Instead of a sentence, the court released the accused after an admonition under Section 562(1-A) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.).
The appellant challenged this decision, arguing that Section 562(1-A) only applies to offences related to property, and wrongful confinement is not such an offence.
law: The legal principle in question is *ejusdem generis*, which suggests that when a general phrase follows a list of specific items, the general phrase should be interpreted as being limited to the same class as the specific items.

Section 562(1-A) of the Cr.P.C. applies to specific offences like "theft, theft in a building, dishonest misappropriation, cheating" followed by the general phrase "or any offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment".
application: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the principle of *ejusdem generis* should apply.
The Court reasoned that the specific offences (theft, cheating, etc.) were not listed to create a limiting class of 'property offences'.

Instead, those specific offences were mentioned precisely because they are punishable with *more* than two years' imprisonment. The legislature had to explicitly include them to make them eligible for treatment under this section.

Therefore, the subsequent general clause, "any offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment," is not restricted by the preceding list. It stands on its own as a separate category.

The Court further reasoned that if the legislature had intended to limit the section's application to only property offences, it could have easily and directly done so by referencing Chapter 17 of the IPC, which covers offences against property.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the phrase 'any offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment' is not limited to property-related offences. It stands by itself and covers all offences under the IPC that fit the punishment criteria, regardless of their nature. Thus, the section was correctly applied to the offence of wrongful confinement.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the phrase 'any offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment' in Section 562(1-A) of the Criminal Procedure Code should be interpreted ejusdem generis with the preceding specific offences, thereby limiting its application to offences relating to property.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (the complainant) argued that Section 562(1-A) of the Criminal Procedure Code is not applicable to an offence under Section 342 of the Indian Penal Code (wrongful confinement).

The appellant contended that Section 562(1-A) is concerned only with offences relating to property, and therefore, offences not concerning property cannot be subjected to treatment under that section.
respondent_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the arguments made by the respondent (the accused). However, their position, by implication, was that the application of Section 562(1-A) to the offence of wrongful confinement was correct and that the section is not limited to property-related offences.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The clause "any offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment" in Section 562(1-A) of the Criminal Procedure Code stands by itself and is not to be read ejusdem generis with the specific offences (like theft) mentioned earlier in the section. This clause indicates that all offences under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment are capable of being dealt with under that section.
obiter: If the legislature had intended to limit the operation of Section 562(1-A) to offences against property, it could have easily specified Chapter 17 of the Indian Penal Code.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the phrase 'any offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment' in Section 562(1-A) of the Criminal Procedure Code is not to be interpreted ejusdem generis with the preceding specific offences. The clause stands by itself and encompasses all offences under the IPC punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment, regardless of whether they relate to property.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's argument that the general words 'any offence under the Indian Penal Code' should be read ejusdem generis with the specific property-related offences mentioned earlier in the section.

The court reasoned that the specific offences like theft and cheating were mentioned precisely because they are punishable with more than two years' imprisonment; it was necessary to explicitly list them to bring them within the section's ambit.

The court noted that if the legislature's intent was to limit the section to offences against property, it could have easily and simply referred to Chapter 17 of the Indian Penal Code, which it did not do.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the respondent's implied position by holding that the clause 'any offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than two years' imprisonment' stands by itself.

The court's structural analysis of the section—that the specific offences were listed due to their higher penalties—supported the conclusion that the subsequent general clause was not meant to be limited by them.
